historical_references.context: Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) was a renowned Arab historian and philosopher. In his magnum opus, 'Muqaddimah' or 'Prolegomena', he wrote about the importance of understanding the sociological, economic and psychological aspects of human societies. He identified a group of Bedouin tribes known as 'Asir and Banu Farhun' or 'Banu Farhun al-Asiri', who lived around the Red Sea coast of Yemen and southern Saudi Arabia. The term 'Farhuni' or 'Farhi' was used to denote their religious leaders, who were considered to be strict adherents of the Islamic faith.

In it, he described the scholars and theological debates of his time. He mentioned a theological disputation between the Hanbali scholar Ibn Taymiyyah and the Shafi'i scholar Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya. One of the Hanbali scholars who supported Ibn Taymiyyah in this debate was named Al-Farhani, who was known for his strong adherence to the Hanbali school of thought.
